title: Catholic: sacred reading
hook: read, reflect, pray and rest on one short passage

segments.voice: Yesterday: the saints. Your line was a cloud of witnesses. Whose face came to mind in your hard mile? Day two hundred sixty-three.

How do you read now? Honestly. Headlines, captions, the first line of an email, the top of a thread. Eyes move in a quick zigzag, hunting for the point, and then they're gone. It's efficient. It also means a whole day of words can pass through and leave almost nothing behind. Now a medieval monk, with one page in front of him, reading it so slowly he's almost chewing it. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: lectio divina, sacred reading.
screen: `SKIM, ZIGZAG, GONE.` → `A DAY OF WORDS, NOTHING LEFT.` → `A MONK, CHEWING ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, or sacred reading. It's old. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks, sets aside hours every day for holy reading. Much later, a Carthusian monk named Guigo wrote a short letter describing the practice as a ladder with four rungs. The first rung is lectio, reading: slowly, often aloud, a short passage, not a chapter. The second is meditatio, reflecting: you turn one word or phrase over and over, chewing on it. Guigo uses that very picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, meditation chews it. The third is oratio, prayer: you respond, speaking to God from what you heard. The fourth is contemplatio, contemplation: you stop working and simply rest in God's presence, beyond words. He also puts it this way: seek in reading and you'll find in meditation; knock in prayer and contemplation opens the door. Here's a line to try it on. Psalm 45 in the Douay-Rheims numbering, 46 in most others: "Be still and see that I am God." Read it once. Then again, and notice which word catches: still, or see, or God. Stay with that word. Answer it, if you pray. Then stop, and be still. In 2010 Pope Benedict the Sixteenth encouraged the practice for all Catholics, not just monks, and Christians of other churches use it too. The point is not to cover ground. It's to let one short passage cover you.
screen: `LECTIO — READ IT SLOWLY.` · `MEDITATIO — CHEW ON ONE WORD.` · `ORATIO — ANSWER.` · `CONTEMPLATIO — REST.` · then, large: `READ SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse four times. Use today's line: be still and see that I am God. First time, just hear it. Second time, notice the one word that catches. Third time, answer it, in prayer if you pray, or in a thought if you don't. Fourth time, let the words go, and simply rest. The bell holds the time.
Lectio divina. Sacred reading: read, reflect, pray, rest, four rungs of a ladder on one short passage. Today's word.
Your line: read slowly. Today, pick one short thing you'd normally skim, a poem, a message, a verse, and read it twice as slowly as usual. Day two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns set aside time for lectio divina each day, and many Catholic parishes and other Christians use it in groups, often with the Sunday Gospel: reading a passage several times, sharing a word, praying, and resting in silence.

look it up in a dictionary.
fork.reveal: that's meditatio: chewing one word. then answer, then rest. seek in reading, find in meditation.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading the Bible.
what it means: reading one short passage slowly, then reflecting, praying and resting in it.
what a scholar hears: the Rule of Benedict's daily lectio; Guigo II's Scala Claustralium, 'the ladder of monks', names the four rungs.

notes: Douay-Rheims Psalm 45:11: confirm exact wording ('Be still and see that I am God').
Guigo II's letter is usually dated to the later twelfth century; the script says 'around the eleven-hundreds'. Confirm.
Guigo's summary ('reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes') is paraphrased from the Scala Claustralium.
Verbum Domini 86–87 (2010) on lectio divina: confirm reference.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Guigo's summary was misquoted ('reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes'); now paraphrases his actual seek/find/knock/open line, and the chewing image is credited to Guigo instead of the overstated 'cow chewing its cud ... really how the monks described it'. Cut the hook's invented statistic ('a thousand words a day') and 'most of us skim', and the uncited dates (sixth century, eleven-hundreds, twelfth century).
